axes.model_access:
**Models from multiple vendors are selectable; the difference between the three personal tiers is allowance multiples, not which models are available.**

**The selectable range listed on the official homepage**:

- OpenAI / Anthropic / Gemini / SpaceXAI / Cursor in-house

The supply side is explicitly more than one vendor: the navigation includes Grok / Grok Bot, and each tier lists a separate "Grok usage allowance".

Auto-mode candidates (official-site example, 2026-10-01):

- Grok 4.7
- GPT-5.6 Sol
- Fable 5.1
- Max Opus 5.5
- Gemini 3.1 Pro
- Composer 2.5

**Allowance mechanism (rolling re-check 2026-10-23: the scheme has switched)**:

The old scheme was monthly allowance multiples (Pro=extended, Pro+=3x, Ultra=20x);
the official pricing page now uses **one usage pool per tier, shared across Cursor and Grok, refreshed weekly**
(official wording: "allowance refreshes weekly").

⚠ **After the switch, model availability became a tier difference**: Plus includes Grok models only
("Plus includes Grok models only"); Premium and above give generous Grok usage
but still do not include an allowance for third-party models ("do not include an allowance for third-party models").
**This is the opposite of the old conclusion that "the difference is only in allowance multiples, not model availability".**

**Cursor Router routes across models in three modes: cost / balance / intelligence.**
The official docs say billing follows the list price of whichever model gets routed to.
The Router launched first on Teams / Enterprise; personal tiers follow "in a few months".
axes.runtime:
**Two run modes: cloud, or self-hosted on your own machines.**

This is the most distinctive architecture in this section.

Official self-hosting support launched 2026-09-02:

- Codebases, build artifacts and secrets stay on machines running inside your own infrastructure
- Agents handle tool calls locally

There is also the **My Machines** mode:
connect a single laptop or VM to your account, for personal workflows.

**Cursor Router has a wider surface.**
Official docs say it works in the editor / CLI / Cursor SDK / iOS app.
axes.local_files:
**The editor mode reads workspace files; in the self-hosted mode code and artifacts never leave your infrastructure.**

It derives from VS Code, so file access works the way an editor's does.

**The indexing strategy is documented officially (added 2026-10-03, from the official Search docs page).**

Retrieval uses the in-house **Instant Grep**.
The official page claims it beats `ripgrep` on large codebases, with no configuration.

**Official wording**: "runs automatically; no configuration needed".

**One data-boundary point worth recording separately:**

**Official wording**: "Instant Grep **builds and queries its index on your machine**. Cursor does not upload file paths or code to build a search index, and it **does not store embeddings of your codebase for search**".

In other words: the search index stays entirely on your machine, and the official page explicitly says it stores no embeddings of your codebase for search.

⚠ But the same page adds right after:

**Official wording**: "When Agent opens a match, **that file content can still be included in the model request**".

So **"indexing stays local" ≠ "file content stays local"**.
Once a match is opened, the content still goes into the model request.

**The Explore subagent is the official context-control mechanism**:

- Runs in a separate context window
- Uses a faster model
- After parallel searches it **returns only the relevant findings**

**Official wording**: "returning only the relevant findings".
The official page says this is to avoid dumping raw file contents into the main conversation.

⚠ **Indexing performance and scale limits on large repos: the official docs give no numbers.**
axes.background:
**Cloud agents keep running without your computer, and the official wording is explicit.**

"Projects" run on dedicated cloud machines — **closing the laptop does not interrupt them**.

When local testing is needed, the orchestrator agent spins up local agents.

**The official page also says the orchestrator can act proactively**:

- Listen to Slack channels
- Run on schedules
- Track all PRs

That is, it acts **without waiting for a prompt**.
axes.tools:
**MCP, Skills and Hooks each have an official page.**

⚠ The old entry said "available from Pro+" — that phrasing came from the old pricing page's feature list;
at the 2026-10-23 rolling re-check the tiers had already switched (see the "Tier structure" section),
and neither the new pricing page nor the MCP docs page marks a tier gate for these three features.
**This site has not verified the availability of these three features under the new tiers.**
**Bugbot is agent-driven code review.**

Teams also has a team marketplace for internal rules, skills and plugins.

**MCP integration details (added 2026-10-03, from the official MCP docs page).**

**Three transports**:

- `stdio`: local, launched by Cursor; can start via a shell command; manual auth
- `SSE`: local, or deployed remotely as a server; multi-user; OAuth
- `Streamable HTTP`: same as `SSE`, local or deployed remotely as a server; multi-user; OAuth

**All six protocol capabilities are supported**:

- Tools / Prompts / Resources / Roots / Elicitation / Apps

**Configuration lives in two layers**:

- Project-level `.cursor/mcp.json`, supports `${workspaceFolder}`
- Global `~/.cursor/mjsson`, supports `${userHome}`

**Four variable interpolations are supported**:

- `${env:NAME}`
- `${userHome}`
- `${workspaceFolder}`
- `${pathSeparator}`

`envFile` is also supported, to read secrets from `.env` (stdio only).

⚠ Note: `~` is the home-directory shorthand, unrelated to any tier.

**Tool approval is on by default.**

**Official wording**: "Cursor asks for approval before using MCP tools by default".

A tool-level allowlist can restrict which tools on a given server may run automatically.

**Each MCP server has its own network mode**:

- Allow all / Allowlist / Deny all / **No sandbox**

**Hooks event list (added 2026-10-03, from the official Hooks and plugin reference pages).**

18 agent hooks:

- `sessionStart` `sessionEnd` `preToolUse` `postToolUse`
- `postToolUseFailure` `subagentStart` `subagentStop`
- `beforeShellExecution` `afterShellExecution`
- `beforeMCPExecution` `afterMCPExecution`
- `beforeReadFile` `afterFileEdit`
- `beforeSubmitPrompt` `preCompact` `stop`
- `afterAgentResponse` `afterAgentThought`

There are also Tab hooks:

- `beforeTabFileRead`
- `afterTabFileEdit`

App lifecycle hooks:

- `workspaceOpen`

Hooks are **command-type** and can carry a `matcher` filter.

**Official wording**: `{"command": "./hooks/audit.sh"}`

The official page also offers a TypeScript variant (Bun-powered), for structured I/O and HTTP.
axes.context:
**The core design of "Projects" is long-lived context maintenance.**

The official wording says it does three things:

- Keeps context across work lasting months
- Delegates tasks to thousands of subagents
- Runs periodic work automatically, without prompts

Shared context syncs across multiple cloud and local machines.
Once one agent figures out how to test a service, later agents can reuse it directly.
axes.permissions:
**The security review is a bot, split into two responsibilities.**

**Security Review covers exploitable flaws**:

- Reads each PR with whole-repo context
- Reports exploitable flaws
- Each finding carries a severity, an attack path and a fix suggestion

Checks include injection, auth bypass, secret commits, SSRF, unsafe deserialization,
and dependency changes that introduce known vulnerabilities.

**Code style and quality issues remain Bugbot's job.**

You can also add per-repo rules that Security Review enforces on every PR.
For example, which client external calls must go through, or which tables may not be queried in request handlers.

**Draft PRs are skipped.**
axes.fit:
Good fit for three kinds of people:

- People who need cloud agents and want tasks to keep running with the laptop closed
- People who need long-horizon (months-scale) context maintenance and large-scale subagent orchestration
- **Enterprises whose code cannot leave their own infrastructure** (the self-hosted mode)

The Free tier suits people who want to try agents at low cost: limited allowance + Composer access.

sections.三个近期的架构级变化:
### ① Self-hosting (2026-09-02)

**Official statement** (translated): "Support for [self-hosting], keeping tool execution entirely inside your own network. Your codebase, build artifacts and secrets stay on internal machines running in your infrastructure, with agents handling tool calls locally."

**This one changes the tool's fundamental positioning**:

- Before this, AI coding tools defaulted to shipping your code out
- Cursor now offers a path that does not

The companion **My Machines** mode:

- Connect a single laptop or VM to your account
- For personal workflows

### ② Projects (2026-09-10)

**Official statement** (translated; two sentences on capability): "Projects let you take on larger-scale work — a feature, a migration, or a whole application." "It maintains context across work lasting **as long as months**, delegates tasks to **thousands of** subagents, and runs periodic work automatically **without prompts**."

**Three key designs**:

| Design | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **The orchestrator agent writes no code** | It only plans work, delegates to implementation agents, and hands results back to you for review |
| **Runs on dedicated cloud machines** | **Closing the laptop does not interrupt it**; local agents start only when on-machine testing is needed |
| **Context syncs across machines** | Once one agent works out how to test a service, later agents reuse it directly |

**"Shared context accumulates with the project, making the orchestrator more effective over time"** —
the most explicit long-context design commitment in this section.

The companion subscription mechanics:

- Have the orchestrator listen to Slack channels
- Run on schedules
- Track all PRs

**Acting proactively without waiting for a prompt**.

**Official note: "Projects are currently in beta."**

### ③ Rollouts + Security Review (2026-09-23)

**Two bots, available only on Teams and Enterprise**.

**Rollouts** — deployment-change monitoring:

- Attaches monitoring items to each PR, reading the diff and the systems involved
- **Writes a monitoring plan in the PR** (risks, expected effects, signals to check, instrumentation gaps)
- **The plan is human-editable**; Rollouts adopts the edited version
- Wakes on deployment triggers and acts on logs, metrics and traces
- **Tracks each environment separately** — the same change may pass staging yet get flagged in production
- On detecting a regression, points at the suspected change and notifies the author
- Can open a rollback PR for review, or hand the fix to a cloud agent
- **Does not merge or roll back on its own for now**

**Security Review** — exploitable-flaw review:

- Reads each PR with whole-repo context and posts one review comment
- Checks include: SQL/command/template injection, authentication and authorization bypasses,
  **checks that a refactor stopped executing**, secrets and credentials committed to source,
  SSRF and unvalidated redirects, unsafe deserialization,
  dependency changes introducing known vulnerabilities

- **Traces where user input enters and what it flows through** (taint tracing)
- Each finding carries a severity, an attack path and a fix suggestion
- Supports per-repo rules enforced on every PR
- **Draft PRs are skipped**

**The responsibility boundary is clear**: code style and quality issues remain Bugbot's job.
sections.档位结构（2026-10-23 滚动核验：已换轨为 7 档）:
⚠ **The tier naming and structure switched wholesale** (the old 6 tiers Hobby/Pro/Pro+/Ultra/Teams/Enterprise are retired).
The official pricing page now lists **Free / Plus / Premium / Super / Ultra / Teams / Enterprise**
(price figures are not stored per our D9 rule; see the official pricing page):

| Tier | Key capabilities (official framing) |
|---|---|
| **Free** | Free personal tier (official wording: "Free for individuals") |
| **Plus** | **Grok models only** (official wording: "Plus includes Grok models only"); positioned for light AI users |
| **Premium** | Generous Grok usage, but **no third-party model allowance** (official wording: "do not include an allowance for third-party models") |
| **Super** | Positioned for "daily agent users" |
| **Ultra** | Positioned for "power users" |
| **Teams** | Positioned for collaborating professionals; larger orgs go to Enterprise |
| **Enterprise** | Contact sales: invoicing/wire settlement, pooled usage, advanced security |

**Two mechanism changes that came with the switch** (official FAQ wording):

- **Allowances became a "weekly-refreshed shared pool"**: each tier includes one AI usage pool shared across Cursor and Grok
  (on the Grok side covering Chat/Imagine/Voice/Bot), **allowance refreshes weekly** —
  the old scheme was "monthly allowance multiples (1x/3x/20x)"; the multiple phrasing recorded in older versions of this site is now outdated.
- **The Plus/Premium difference is model availability**: Plus has Grok only; Premium and above give generous Grok usage
  but still no third-party model allowance. **This is the opposite of the old conclusion that "the difference is only in allowance multiples, not model availability"** —
  after the switch, model availability became part of the tier differences.

**Paid tiers include Grok API access**, but API usage is billed separately at standard model prices and does not draw on the plan pool (official FAQ).
